title: Catholic: the rosary
hookLine: beads, prayers, and the stories of Jesus and Mary, one decade at a time

cards: Maybe you've seen one hanging from a rearview mirror. Or wrapped around a grandmother's fingers in a hospital waiting room, her lips moving without a sound. Or laid in the hands of someone at a funeral.
A loop of beads with a small cross at the end. It looks like jewelry, but the people who pray with it say it's something you do, not something you wear.
Its rhythm has carried people through long nights, long drives and long grief. Today: the rosary.

teach.b: The word comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: a garland of prayers offered like roses. Here's how it works. The beads are grouped in tens, called decades, usually five on a rosary.
Each decade begins on a single bead with the Our Father, the prayer from last week.

teach.h: DECADES: ONE OUR FATHER, TEN HAIL MARYS.
teach.b: Then ten Hail Marys, one per bead, a prayer i'll open properly in a few days. Then a short Glory Be. And while the fingers move and the lips repeat, the mind is somewhere else: in a story.

teach.h: EACH DECADE, A MYSTERY TO PONDER.
teach.b: Each decade is paired with a scene from the lives of Jesus and Mary, called a mystery. The joyful mysteries include the angel's visit to Mary and the birth in Bethlehem.
The sorrowful mysteries walk through the arrest and the crucifixion. The glorious mysteries begin with the resurrection.
In 2002, Pope John Paul the Second added a fourth set, the luminous mysteries, from Jesus' public life, like his baptism and the Last Supper.

teach.h: REPETITION FOR THE BODY, STORY FOR THE MIND.
teach.b: So the rosary is two things at once: a repetition for the body and a meditation for the mind. The beads keep count, so you don't have to.
Where did it come from? A popular tradition says Mary gave it to Saint Dominic in the thirteenth century.
Historians tend to see it growing more gradually, out of medieval monks praying the hundred and fifty psalms, and laypeople who couldn't read saying a hundred and fifty short prayers instead.
Either way, it grew up for people with busy hands and no books.

how: Many Catholics pray the rosary daily or weekly, alone or in groups, often praying one set of mysteries assigned to each day of the week; October is traditionally the month of the rosary.

o: a prayer book read aloud at Sunday Mass
prayer beads counted while pondering stories
a cross necklace worn as a sign of faith

games.q: inside the rosary — tap the pairs.

s: it's a way of praying: beads to count, stories to ponder.

games.q: you're a medieval farmer who can't read the hundred and fifty psalms the monks pray. what do you do?
o: say a hundred and fifty short prayers, counted on beads.
pay a monk to pray for you.
games.why: historians trace the rosary in part to laypeople who prayed short prayers in place of the psalms, counting on beads or knots.

practice: Hold beads if you have them; if not, a string with ten knots, or simply your ten fingers. Move through them slowly, one breath per bead: a prayer you know on each one if you pray, or, if not, let each breath be a quiet thank-you.
Let your mind rest on one scene: a birth, a table, a sunrise.

wordCard.voice: Rosary. From rosarium, a rose garden: beads counted in decades, each one carrying a story of Jesus and Mary. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a rose garden, a garland of roses.

carryVoice: Your line: one bead at a time. The big things go the same way, one small piece and then the next. See you tomorrow.
